ABOUT THIS EDITION

The Akan Contemporary Bible, titled "Asante Twi Nkwa Asem" ("The Living Word"), is a complete Bible in the Asante Twi dialect of Akan, published by Biblica, Inc. (formerly International Bible Society). The translation took 24 years, beginning in 1996, and was launched on September 11, 2020, in Kumasi, Ghana, in collaboration with the Kumasi Council of Christian Churches. Key translators include Rev. Walter Aboagye Frimpong and Rev. Dr. Ebenezer Boafo. It is a contemporary, easy-to-read translation designed as an alternative to the older "Twere Kronkron" (the 1964 Asante Twi Bible published by the Bible Society of Ghana).

ABOUT THIS EDITION

The Nkwa Asem (Word of Life) is a contemporary Asante Twi Bible produced by Biblica (the International Bible Society). The New Testament was first published in 1996, and the complete Bible was released in 2020 after decades of translation work. It is made available as an open-licensed text through Biblica's Open.Bible initiative. The translation draws on multiple source texts including the New Living Translation, the New International Version, and the Hebrew and Greek critical editions, aiming for clear, accessible language in contemporary Asante Twi. This translation is distinct from the earlier Twere Kronkron, the formal-equivalence Twi Bible published by the Bible Society of Ghana. Twi Bible translation has deep roots in Ghana: the first complete Twi Bible was published in Basel in 1871 by the German Basel Mission linguist Johann Gottlieb Christaller, working with Ghanaian scholars David Asante, Theophilus Opoku, Jonathan Palmer Bekoe, and Paul Staudt Keteku, using the Akuapem dialect. Christaller's pioneering linguistic work, including his 1875 Twi grammar and 1881 dictionary, laid the foundation for Akan-language literature.

1. The Beginning

Genesis 1:1

1. The Beginning

Genesis 1:1

The story of Jesus fits within the larger story of the Judeo Christian tradition. The purpose of everything since creation has been to point to the life of Jesus. All of creation speaks of the majesty of God. As God created man and woman he intended them to live in peace with him forever. But because of their disobedience mankind was separated from God. But God still loved mankind so throughout the Scriptures God reveals his plan to save the world.

3:43
2. Birth Of Jesus

Luke 1:1

2. Birth Of Jesus

Luke 1:1

Luke makes his introduction as the careful author of this Gospel. The angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a virgin in Nazareth. He announces to her that she has found favor with God and will give birth to Jesus, the Son of God. Through Jesus' birth, prophecies are fulfilled by the arrangement of events. God leaves no detail unnoticed. The same can be said of our own lives.

2:15
3. Childhood Of Jesus

Luke 2:21

3. Childhood Of Jesus

Luke 2:21

One week after the baby is born, He is circumcised and officially named Jesus. While Jesus is a small boy they go to the temple where they meet a man named Simeon. The Holy Spirit had assured Simeon he would not die before seeing the Lord's Messiah. Simeon sees Jesus and declares Him the promised Messiah.

4. Baptism Of Jesus By John

Luke 3:1

4. Baptism Of Jesus By John

Luke 3:1

John the Baptist calls out in the desert. He preaches by the river Jordan, "Turn away from your sins and be baptized, and God will forgive your sins." He is the one Isaiah predicted would make way for the Lord. The crowds gather. Immediately, he warns them not to only say they have repented. Instead, they're to follow repentance with actions that exhibit a changed heart. Jesus is baptized and receives the Holy Spirit. He kneels at the feet of someone lesser than Himself to be baptized. He demonstrates how we are to be humble.

2:22
5. The Devil Tempts Jesus

Luke 4:1

5. The Devil Tempts Jesus

Luke 4:1

After Jesus has been baptized, He's led by the Spirit into the desert. He spends 40 days there, constantly tempted by the devil. All that time, he eats nothing. The devil tries to tempt Jesus, but Jesus answers using Scripture, resisting him.

6. Jesus Proclaims Fulfillment Of The Scriptures

Luke 4:14

6. Jesus Proclaims Fulfillment Of The Scriptures

Luke 4:14

When Jesus returns to Nazareth, He goes to the synagogue. He's asked to read the Scriptures and is handed the Book of Isaiah. From it, He reads Isaiah 61:1-2. The prophecy speaks of bringing good news to the poor, proclaiming liberty to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind, freeing the oppressed, and announcing that it's time the Lord will save His people. When He finishes reading, Jesus announces to the people that the prophecy has come true as it was just read.

7. Parable Of The Pharisee And Tax Collector

Luke 18:9

7. Parable Of The Pharisee And Tax Collector

Luke 18:9

Jesus teaches from a boat off the shore of Lake Gennesaret. He speaks in parables, giving the example of a Pharisee and tax collector going to the temple to pray. The two men approach prayer very differently. The Pharisee in the story stands by himself and lists his respectable attributes. He thanks God that he is not greedy, dishonest, or an adulterer like everyone else. He specifically points out the tax collector and thanks God for not being like him. The Pharisee boldly tells God what he does: He fasts two days a week and gives a tenth of his income. The tax collector stands at a distance from the altar. Head bowed, he beats on his chest. The only thing he prays is, "God, have pity on me, a sinner!"

Luke 5:1

8. Miraculous Catch Of Fish

Luke 5:1

Jesus tells the fisherman who owns it to push out farther and let down their nets. The fisherman grumbles that he and the others have already been out all night long. They didn't catch anything. The fisherman agrees to go out and calls to his partners. Jesus sits in the boat with the fisherman. He waits expectantly. Then gathers the nets, slowly bringing something to the surface. He laughs with joy when he sees the nets are full of flopping fish. When they're done, the fisherman sits in a boat full of fish. He looks up to Jesus. The fisherman frowns and says, "Go away from me, Lord. I am a sinful man." Jesus tells him not to be afraid, that from then on, he would be a fisher of men.

9. Jairuss Daughter Brought Back To Life

Luke 8:41

9. Jairuss Daughter Brought Back To Life

Luke 8:41

Crowds press in on Jesus as He leaves the synagogue. One voice rises above the others. A man, Jairus, begs Jesus to save his sick, 12-year-old daughter. Another man runs up to Jairus. He tells him not to bother the teacher, that his daughter has died. Jesus turns and tells him not to be afraid. And that if Jairus would believe, his daughter would be well. Jesus and the disciples visit the family. The neighbors wail for the loss of the daughter. She lies lifeless on a cot. Jesus looks at her for a moment. Then He looks to the child’s mother and comforts her. He says the child isn't dead, but that she’s actually just asleep. Jesus sits and looks at the girl for a moment, then tells her to rise.

10. Disciples Chosen

Luke 5:27

10. Disciples Chosen

Luke 5:27

Jesus spots a tax collector named Matthew Levi at the gate. He collects toll money for customs as people pass through. As Jesus looks at him, Matthew senses it and looks up. Jesus says, "Follow me." Matthew watches Him go for a moment. Silently, he stands and leaves everything to follow Jesus. Later Jesus goes up a hill to pray. He prays the entire night to God. When He comes down from the hill the next morning, He gathers His followers. From them, he chooses 12 apostles. Simon (who Jesus named Peter) and Simon's brother Andrew had been the fishermen who experienced the miracle of a large catch of fish. Then Jesus chooses James and John, Philip and Bartholomew. And He chooses Matthew, the tax collector he had called at the gate. And finally Jesus chooses Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who would betray Jesus.

11. Beatitudes

Luke 6:20

11. Beatitudes

Luke 6:20

Jesus looks out over the crowds gathered to hear him speak. But instead of speaking to the masses, Jesus turns back to his disciples. He encourages them for the journey ahead. He assures them that they are blessed when people hate them, reject them, insult them, and say that they are evil because they follow Jesus. He encourages them to be happy and dance for joy when that happens. Because there will be great reward in heaven for them. And He reminds them that their ancestors acted the same way toward prophets.

12. Sermon On The Mount

Luke 6:24

Jesus turns to the crowds and walks through them, teaching. He advises everyone how to walk through life in love. And talks of how, out of pride, we often judge others. He implores those who are listening to love their enemies, to actively pray for them. He speaks of offering more than what is asked of you. Do for others what you would have them do for you.

13. Blessed Are Those Who Hear And Obey

A Pharisee invites Jesus to have dinner at His house. They're eating when a woman approaches Jesus. Everyone in the house stares, including the Pharisee. Jesus tells the Pharisee a story. He says that there were two men who owed money to someone. One owed 500 silver coins. The other owed 50. Neither men could pay their debt. So the lender canceled both debts. Jesus asks which man loved the lender more for what he'd done.

15. Women Disciples

And the boat starts to take on water. The whole time, Jesus stays asleep. The disciples hold on tight. They try to keep the boat afloat. Finally, Peter cries out to the still sleeping Jesus. He tells Jesus that the boat is taking on water and that they'll all be drowned. Jesus stands and puts a hand out toward the storm. The storm clears. And the seas immediately calm.

The man threatens Jesus with the rock. But Jesus just continues to stare at him. The man calls Jesus by name and declares Him to be the Son of God. Jesus asks him his name. Jesus puts a hand out to the pigs.

Jesus and the disciples continue to walk the countryside. And a great crowd follows them. Peter comes and asks Jesus to send the people away. Jesus considers this and tells the disciples to feed the people. Mary Magdalene points out that they only have a few loaves of bread and two fish. Jesus takes the baskets and proclaims to the heavens and the people, "Blessed is the Lord God, King of the Universe who brings forth bread from the earth."

Jesus asks who the crowds say He is. Peter speaks up immediately. He claims that some in the crowds say Jesus is John the Baptist. Others say He's Elijah. Jesus stares back at him.

23. The Transfiguration

Jesus takes John, James and Peter up a hill to pray. Jesus walks apart from them, covering His head to pray. But when He does, His appearance changes. His face changes. His clothes become pure white. He starts talking to two men who seem to be with Him. Moses and Elijah speak to Him. One says Jesus will fulfill God's purpose. The other says He will die in Jerusalem. Peter slowly wakes up. He's the first to see Moses and Elijah talking with Jesus. He wakes James and John. They see it too. Moses and Elijah turn and leave, fading away. The disciples fall to their knees and worship Jesus.

Jesus gently tells the man to bring his son closer. Two men carry the boy to Jesus. But he falls again into another fit. Jesus comes to stand over him. The boy looks up. And slowly, he gets up. Now, where there were cuts and bruises on his face, there are none.

25. The Lords Prayer

his 1964 Akan Genesis portion bears the vernacular title Mose Nhoma a Edi Kan, "the first book of Moses", and reproduces the opening book of the Old Testament in Twi for Akan-speaking readers in southern Ghana. The edition was prepared by the Bible Society of Ghana, which was constituted as an autonomous body under the United Bible Societies in 1965, with preparatory work carried out in the early 1960s by staff inherited from the former British and Foreign Bible Society agency in Accra.

The Twi biblical tradition in Ghana goes back to the Basel Mission. Johann Gottlieb Christaller's Twi New Testament appeared in 1864 and the complete Akuapem-Twi Bible in 1871. An Asante-Twi Bible followed in stages through the early twentieth century. By the 1960s the Bible Society was producing selective reprints and school-edition portions of Genesis, Exodus, and the Gospels for use in Presbyterian and Methodist primary schools, where Twi was the medium of religious instruction.

This Genesis booklet belongs to that school and catechumen program. It carries the Akuapem-Twi orthography standardized by Christaller and revised in 1944 by the Akan Orthography Committee, with tone marks omitted in the running text. Children and new literates in the church schools of the 1960s used booklets of this kind before encountering the full Bible.

Akan today is spoken by about eleven million people across Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.

he Akuapem Twi Bible is the foundational Scripture translation for the Akan language cluster of southern Ghana. The complete Bible was first published in 1871 under the direction of Johann Gottlieb Christaller of the Basel Mission, with the New Testament having appeared in 1864. Christaller worked at Akropong in the Akuapem ridge north of Accra, basing the translation on the dialect of the Akuapem royal town because of its relative phonological clarity and its central role in early mission schooling.

Christaller was assisted by Akan-speaking catechists, among them David Asante, Theophilus Opoku, Paul Keteku, and Jonathan Palmer Bekoe, whose local knowledge shaped the idiomatic register of the text. The translation followed decades of linguistic groundwork, including Christaller's 1875 Grammar of the Asante and Fante Language and his 1881 dictionary, both of which drew directly on the translation work and remain standard references today.

The Akuapem Bible became the liturgical standard for the Presbyterian Church of Ghana, the successor of the Basel Mission work, and served as a reference point for later translations into Asante Twi (1964) and Fante. Revised editions have been issued by the Bible Society of Ghana through the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Akuapem Twi is spoken by roughly 600,000 people as a primary dialect and is understood by several million more across the wider Akan continuum (Ethnologue: aka).

he Akuapem Twi New Testament of 1870 is the first complete Akan New Testament, translated by Johann Gottlieb Christaller with the Ghanaian scholars David Asante and Theophilus Opoku for the Basel Mission. Akuapem Twi is one of three main literary dialects of Akan (ISO 639-3 aka), spoken in the Akuapem ridge north of Accra, and the dialect the Basel Mission selected as its written standard after establishing the Akropong seminary in 1848.

Christaller arrived on the Gold Coast in 1853, served the mission inland at Akropong and Aburi, and returned to Basel in 1868 to supervise printing. His New Testament appeared in 1870 from the Basel Mission Press. He completed the Old Testament by 1871, with the full Bible issued in 1871-1872. Christaller's companion works, the Dictionary of the Asante and Fante Language called Tshi (1881) and the Grammar of the Asante and Fante Language (1875), established Twi as a written language with codified orthography, including the use of ɔ and ɛ for the open vowels, which remain part of the modern Akan alphabet.

David Asante, son of the chief of Akropong, was the first Ghanaian ordained to the Basel Mission ministry (1862) and a principal translator; Theophilus Opoku, also from Akuapem, joined the revision after completing theological studies at Basel. Their New Testament was reprinted through the late nineteenth century and into the twentieth by the Basel Mission and the BFBS and remained the Presbyterian Church of Ghana's standard Scripture until the 1964 revision.

his 1905 New Testament represents the Basel Mission tradition of Twi (Akan) Scripture, rooted in the translation work of Johann Gottlieb Christaller at Akropong-Akuapem in the second half of the nineteenth century. Christaller, trained at Basel and assigned to the Gold Coast in 1853, completed the Twi New Testament in 1864 and the full Bible in 1871, working with Ghanaian catechists David Asante, Theophilus Opoku, and Jonathan Palmer Bekoe. His Twi grammar of 1875 and his Twi-English dictionary of 1881 remain foundational works on the language.

The 1905 edition reflects later Basel Mission revisions to Christaller's text. It presents the Twi New Testament in the Akuapem literary form that Christaller established as the written standard, and the title pages of copies from this period sometimes identified it as "Fante-Tshi" to indicate the broader Akan audience targeted by the Basel orthography.

The Basel Mission press, operating from Basel and from the mission's field presses on the Gold Coast, distributed the text through schools and congregations linked to what became the Presbyterian Church of Ghana. By 1905 Twi Scripture was in active circulation among Akan communities from Akuapem through Asante, and subsequent revisions separated the Fante and Twi traditions into distinct published Bibles.

The 1905 printing preserves the Christaller text that shaped Akan literary culture and remains the ancestor of modern Twi Scripture editions.

he complete Bible in Asante Twi was first published in 1964 by the Bible Society of Ghana within the United Bible Societies family, following nearly a century of scripture work in the closely related Akan varieties. Asante Twi is one of the two major literary dialects of the Akan language group (ISO 639-3 twi / aka), spoken by around three million people with the Ashanti Region as its heartland. Akuapem Twi had received the earlier Basel Mission scripture treatment (J. G. Christaller's Akuapem Twi Bible of 1871), and for decades Asante readers used that edition despite its dialectal distance.

The Asante project was taken up in the mid-twentieth century as African church leadership matured and the desirability of a dedicated Asante text became clear. A translation committee drawn from the Presbyterian, Methodist, and Anglican churches in Kumasi worked through the mid-century, drawing on the Akuapem Bible and on Christaller's foundational Twi dictionary and grammar while bringing the diction and orthography into Asante usage.

The 1964 edition was printed and distributed by the Bible Society and quickly became the standard pulpit and household Bible in Ashanti. A revised Asante Twi Bible (Twere Kronkron) has been produced in subsequent decades, and the Bible Society of Ghana has continued to issue portion editions, study Bibles, and audio recordings in Asante Twi. Today Asante Twi scripture, together with Akuapem and Fante editions, serves the largest language community of Ghana.

he Asante Gospel of John is part of the Twi-Akan scriptural programme of the Basel Mission on the Gold Coast (modern Ghana), centred on the philological work of Johann Gottlieb Christaller. Christaller arrived at Akropong in 1853 as a Württemberg missionary and turned to the systematic study of Akuapem Twi and Asante Twi under the guidance of the native catechists David Asante and Theophilus Opoku.

Christaller's Akuapem New Testament appeared in 1864 and his full Bible in 1871, both printed at the Basel Mission press. The Asante variant, represented in this Gospel of John, adapts the Akuapem text to the Asante dialect spoken in Kumasi and the interior. The Yohane Nkyerɛkyerɛ was issued in portions from the late 1860s as the mission extended inland from its coastal stations at Akropong, Aburi, and Christiansborg.

The text uses the orthography Christaller codified in his Dictionary of the Asante and Fante Language of 1881 and his Grammar of the Asante and Fante Language of 1875, retaining tone marks and the special characters ɔ and ɛ. David Asante, son of the Akropong chief and the first African ordained by the Basel Mission, assisted with the Asante renderings and later produced a fuller dialectal revision published after his death in 1892.

his Asante (Twi) New Testament shares text and abbreviation with the 1905 Basel Mission printing catalogued under the same abbr. The translation line runs from Johann Gottlieb Christaller's 1864 New Testament and 1871 full Bible, produced at Akropong-Akuapem with the Ghanaian catechists David Asante, Theophilus Opoku, and Jonathan Palmer Bekoe. The Basel Mission's orthographic decisions, settled in Christaller's Twi grammar of 1875 and Twi dictionary of 1881, governed the written form that all subsequent Akan Bibles adopted.

The edition presents the standard twenty-seven books in the Akuapem literary form that the Basel Mission had established for Twi publishing. Copies circulated through Presbyterian congregations on the Gold Coast, which traced their origin to the Basel work and which became the Presbyterian Church of Ghana.

For the canonical description of this translation under abbr AKA1905, see the companion record Asante-1905-New-Testament-Fante-Tshi. That entry carries the fuller account of Christaller's translation history, the Basel Mission press, and the spread of Twi Scripture from Akuapem through the Akan-speaking regions.

his 1964 Genesis portion in Asante Twi was produced by the Bible Society of Ghana with BFBS support for the Asante-speaking populations of the Ashanti Region of Ghana. Asante Twi is one of the principal varieties of Akan (ISO 639-3 aka as a macrolanguage, with Asante commonly tagged asa in the Bible Society cataloguing), a Kwa language of the Niger-Congo family, spoken by roughly 3.8 million first-language Asante users and comprehensible to the wider Akan community of some 20 million.

Akan scripture translation was shaped by the Basel Mission on the Gold Coast from the 1840s. Johann Gottlieb Christaller, arriving at Akropong in 1853, produced the monumental Akuapem Twi Bible of 1871, a landmark of African-language biblical and lexicographic scholarship. A separate Asante Twi translation followed in the twentieth century, recognizing the dialectal and literary distinctiveness of the Asante heartland. The Asante Twi Bible of 1964, sponsored by the Bible Society of Ghana with BFBS consultancy, established the current Asante ecclesiastical text used by the Presbyterian, Methodist, Catholic, and Pentecostal churches across Ashanti.

This 1964 Genesis portion, issued alongside or shortly after the complete Asante Twi Bible, is a paperbound small-format Bible Society booklet printed in Roman orthography using the Asante Twi tone and vowel conventions. It served congregational reading, Sunday School, and literacy classes across the Ashanti Region in the immediate post-independence period.

his Fante Gospel of John is a Bible Society of Ghana portion in the Fante dialect of Akan (ISO 639-3 fat), spoken by about three million people along the coast of Ghana's Central Region between Winneba and Sekondi-Takoradi. Fante is one of the three main literary dialects of Akan, alongside Asante Twi and Akuapem Twi, and carries its own orthography and literary tradition rooted in the Wesleyan Methodist mission that established itself at Cape Coast from 1835.

The Methodist missionary Thomas Birch Freeman and his Ghanaian colleagues produced early Fante portions in the mid-nineteenth century, and a Fante New Testament appeared in 1896 through BFBS. A revised Fante Bible was issued in the twentieth century and then further revised by the Bible Society of Ghana, which published a common-language Fante Bible in the 1990s and subsequent editions. The Fante orthography uses the pan-Akan letters ɔ and ɛ alongside standard Latin characters.

The Gospel of John printing in this collection is a Bible Society of Ghana single-portion issue designed for school, church, and evangelistic distribution in the Fante heartland along the Cape Coast corridor. It retains the distinctive Fante Methodist vocabulary for key theological terms (Nyame, Kristo, asaase) that sets it apart from the Asante and Akuapem Twi editions.
